title: Mitigating Overgeneralization in RND via Spectral Target Design
claim: The standard novelty signal fails in a systematic way: it assigns low scores to unfamiliar inputs far from the data, overlapping with scores for familiar inputs.
layout: 2 panels, left heatmap with contours, right overlapping histograms, shared region colors
description: Two-panel diagnostic figure. Panel (a) is a 2-D heatmap of RND energy over x1 and x2 in [-2, 2], drawn with a dark-to-bright magma colormap and a colorbar scaled by 10^4. Blue training points form a noisy ring. A blue dashed contour hugs the ring (r_in), and a red dash-dotted contour (r_out) encloses an inner hole and also appears outside the ring. The central hole is dark and labeled in bold red 'low E (failure)'. Energy rises toward the bright corners. Panel (b) shows overlaid histograms of energy by region. Blue (covered) and red (interior hole) bars pile up at nearly the same low-energy values, with dashed vertical lines marking each group. The gray exterior distribution sits at higher energy and runs off the right edge. The eye goes first to the red-labeled dark hole and the ring.
caption: Coverage-based diagnostic for standard RND on S1 data. (a) RND energy heatmap with contours defined by ρD(x) = minxi∈D dX (x, xi). The blue dashed contour denotes ρD = rin, and the red dash-dotted contour denotes ρD = rout. The interior hole (“low E (failure)”) lies beyond the coverage radius but receives low RND energy. (b) Energy distributions by region. The covered band (blue, ρD ≤rin) and the interior hole (red, ρD ≥rout) have overlapping low-energy distributions, illustrating a failure of coverage-based residual separation. The exterior region (gray) is shown only for reference. Energies are scaled by 104 for visualization since the trained RND energies are small.
abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.
